title: Chapter 18 — Of The Inflated Style Of American Writers And Orators
paragraphs: I have often noticed that the Americans, who generally treat business in clear, plain language, devoid of any ornament, and so extremely simple as to be often coarse, are apt to become inflated as soon as they attempt a more poetic diction. They then vent their pomposity from one end of a speech to the other. To hear them lavish imagery on every occasion, one might imagine they never spoke of anything with simplicity. The English are more rarely given to a similar failing. The cause of this can be pointed out without much difficulty. In democratic communities, each citizen is habitually occupied with the contemplation of a very puny object — namely, himself. If he ever raises his eyes higher, he then sees nothing but the immense form of society at large, or the still more imposing aspect of mankind. His ideas are either extremely small and clear, or extremely general and vague. What lies between is an open void. So when he has been drawn out of his own sphere, he always expects some amazing object to be offered to his attention. And it is only on these terms that he consents to tear himself for a moment from the petty complicated cares that form the charm and the excitement of his life. This seems to me enough to explain why people in democracies, whose concerns are in general so paltry, call upon their poets for conceptions so vast and descriptions so unlimited.

The authors, for their part, do not fail to obey an inclination they themselves share. They continually inflate their imaginations and, expanding them beyond all bounds, they not infrequently abandon the great in order to reach the gigantic. By these means they hope to attract the attention of the multitude and to fix it easily upon themselves. Nor are their hopes disappointed. For since the multitude looks for nothing in poetry but subjects of very vast dimensions, it has neither the time to measure accurately the proportions of all the subjects set before it, nor a taste correct enough to perceive at once in what respect they are out of proportion. The author and the public corrupt one another.

We have just seen that among democratic nations the sources of poetry are grand but not abundant. They are soon exhausted. And poets, not finding the elements of the ideal in what is real and true, abandon them entirely and create monsters. I do not fear that the poetry of democratic nations will prove too insipid, or that it will fly too close to the ground. I rather fear that it will forever lose itself in the clouds, and will at last range into purely imaginary regions. I fear that the productions of democratic poets may often be overloaded with immense and incoherent imagery, with exaggerated descriptions and strange creations — and that the fantastic beings of their brain may sometimes make us regret the world of reality.
